title: Variables
subtitle: Input → transformation → output
idea: Every program is input → transformation → output. Variables are labeled boxes that hold values while the transformation happens.

prose.text: Forget everything mystical about code. A program takes something **in**, changes it, and puts something **out**. A variable is just a labeled box — you put a value in the box, the label lets you find it later.

Four types you'll use constantly: `str` (text), `int` (whole numbers), `float` (decimals), `bool` (`True`/`False`). Python figures out the type from the value — you don't declare it. The `=` sign **stores**, it doesn't mean "equals" like in math.

`input()` **pauses and waits** for the user to type — that's the input. `.upper()` transforms the text — that's the transformation. `print()` shows the result — that's the output. Every program you'll ever write is this shape with fancier steps.

examples.title: Boxes with labels — and every value has a type:
examples.code:
name = "Chauncey"
age = 34
price = 9.99
paid = False

print(name, type(name))
print(age, type(age))
print(price, type(price))
print(paid, type(paid))

examples.title: The full model — input, transform, output:
examples.code:
name = input("Your name: ")
shout = name.upper()
print("Hello,", shout + "!")

exercises.task: Ask the user for two whole numbers and print their sum.
exercises.hint: input() always returns text, even when the user types digits. int() turns text like "42" into the number 42. You'll need it twice.

title: Decisions & repetition
subtitle: if, for, while
idea: if lets the program choose a path. for and while let it repeat. Choice plus repetition is the entire trick behind everything software appears to be "smart" at.

prose.text: A program that runs top-to-bottom with no choices is a recipe. Two ideas turn recipes into machines: **decisions** (do this OR that) and **repetition** (do it again).

The `if` line is the question. The **indented** lines underneath run only when the answer is yes. `elif` means "else, if this instead" — checked only when everything above was no. `else` is the fallback. Indentation isn't style here, it's **structure**: it decides what belongs to the question.

`names` is a **list** — boxes in a row (Lesson 4 goes deep). The loop takes each item, calls it `name` for one round, and runs the indented block. Three names, three hellos, one block of code. The `if` inside shows the real shape of programs: **loops with decisions inside**.

`for` is for "each item in this collection". `while` is for "keep going until something changes". Every `while` needs a line that moves toward the exit (`n = n - 1`) — without it, the loop never ends and you meet your first **infinite loop**. (Ctrl-C kills it.)

examples.title: Decisions — the program asks a yes/no question:
Repetition over a collection:
examples.output:
Hello, boss: Ava
Hello, Ben
Hello, Cy

examples.title: while repeats until a condition breaks:
examples.code:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
print("go")

exercises.task: Print the numbers 1 to 20, but print the word "even" instead of each even number.
exercises.hint: range(1, 21) gives 1..20. n % 2 is the remainder after dividing by 2 — it equals 0 exactly when n is even.

title: Functions
subtitle: Name it once, use it everywhere
idea: A function is a named chunk of recipe. Data goes in through parameters, results come out through return. Define once, call anywhere.

prose.text: The moment you copy-paste a block of code a second time, it wants to be a function. You give the chunk a name, list what it needs as **parameters**, and hand the answer back with **return**.

`def` draws the boundary. `name` and `days` are parameters — empty slots that get filled by whoever calls. `return` hands the finished string **back to the caller**. The function doesn't print; it returns, and the caller decides what to do with the result.

`print` shows a human a value and throws it away. `return` gives the value to the program so it can be stored (`x = double(21)`), chained (`double(double(2))`), or tested. Rule: **functions return, scripts print.**

examples.title: Define once, call in a loop:
examples.output:
Hi Ava, invoice due in 3 days.
Hi Ben, invoice due in 3 days.

examples.title: return vs print — the confusion that bites everyone once:
examples.code:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

x = double(21)
print(x)
print(double(double(2)))

exercises.task: Write total(numbers) — a function that takes a list of numbers and returns their sum.
exercises.hint: Start with t = 0. Loop over the list, add each number to t. Return t — after the loop ends, so check your indentation.

title: Lists & tuples
subtitle: Ordered collections
idea: A list is an ordered row of boxes you can change. A tuple is the same row, locked. Position matters — counting starts at 0.

prose.text: One variable holds one value. A **list** holds many, in order. A **tuple** holds many, in order, permanently — use it when the data shouldn't change out from under you.

Indexing starts at **0** — `appts[0]` is the first item. Negative indexes count from the end (`-1` is last). Slices take a range: `appts[1:]` means "from position 1 to the end". `.append()` grows the list. `len()` counts it.

`x, y = point` is **unpacking** — Python splits the tuple into variables in one move. You'll see this everywhere: functions returning two values, loops over pairs. Trying `point[0] = 99` would crash — that's the lock doing its job.

examples.title: Lists: index, slice, grow:
examples.code:
appts = ["9:00 Ava", "10:30 Ben"]
appts.append("12:00 Cy")
print(len(appts))
print(appts[0])
print(appts[-1])
print(appts[1:])

examples.title: Tuples: locked, and unpacking:
examples.code:
point = (10, 20)
print(point[0])
x, y = point
print("x =", x, " y =", y)

exercises.task: Reverse a list without using .reverse() or reversed().
exercises.hint: Slicing takes an optional step: items[start:stop:step]. A step of -1 walks backwards.

title: Dictionaries
subtitle: Look things up by name
idea: A dictionary is labeled drawers: you fetch values by key (a name), not by position. It's the shape of almost every real record — invoices, users, configs.

prose.text: Lists answer "what's third?" Dictionaries answer "what's the client's name?" — you look things up by **key** instead of counting positions. Nearly every record in real software (an invoice, a user, a config) is a dictionary.

`invoice["client"]` opens the drawer labeled `"client"`. Two ways to read: brackets **demand** the key exists (missing key = crash), `.get()` asks politely and takes a fallback. Rule of thumb: brackets when the key *must* be there, `.get()` when it might not be.

`.items()` gives key-and-value together — unpack them straight into two loop variables. `.keys()` and `.values()` give each side alone. Keys must be unique and unchangeable (strings and numbers are the usual choice).

examples.title: Drawers with labels:
examples.code:
invoice = {"id": "INV-1042", "client": "Ava", "amount": 400, "paid": False}
print(invoice["client"])
print(invoice.get("notes", "no notes"))
invoice["paid"] = True
print(invoice["paid"])

exercises.hint: Split the sentence into words first. Then: counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1 — read it as "whatever was there before (or 0), plus one".

title: Strings in depth
subtitle: Text is a sequence
idea: Text is a sequence of characters — so everything you learned about sequences (indexing, slicing, looping) works on strings, plus purpose-built tools: split, join, strip, and f-strings.

prose.text: You already format text with f-strings. Underneath, a string is a **sequence of characters** — indexable, sliceable, loopable, exactly like a list. Plus a toolbox built for text.

`split("|")` cuts the string at every `|` and returns the pieces as a list — this is how you parse lines from files, CSV-ish data, and pasted records. The f-string then reassembles the pieces in your format.

The greatest hits: `.strip()` trims whitespace, `.lower()`/`.upper()` fix case, `.split()` cuts apart, `"sep".join(list)` glues a list back together with a separator, `.replace()` swaps text. Chain them — `messy.strip().lower()` reads left to right and each step feeds the next.

examples.title: Split a record, rebuild it your way:
examples.code:
record = "Chauncey|Springfield|555-010-0199"
parts = record.split("|")
print(parts)
print(f"{parts[0]} from {parts[1]}: {parts[2]}")

examples.title: Clean and reassemble:
examples.code:
messy = "   hello WORLD   "
print(messy.strip().lower())
print("a,b,c".split(","))
print(" | ".join(["a", "b", "c"]))
print("price: 49".replace("49", "59") )
examples.output:
hello world
['a', 'b', 'c']
a | b | c
price: 59

exercises.hint: Slice it into three pieces — [0:3], [3:6], [6:] — then glue with an f-string and two dashes.

title: Files & persistence
subtitle: Data that survives the program
idea: Variables die when the program ends. Files are how data survives. open() with a with-block is the whole pattern — write it once and reuse it forever.

prose.text: Everything so far evaporates when the script finishes. **Files are memory that outlives the program.** Invoices, logs, configs — all just files your program reads and writes. The pattern never changes:

`"w"` means **write** (creates the file, or wipes it clean first — respect that). The `with` block opens the file and **guarantees it gets closed**, even if something crashes mid-write. Always use it; never leave a file hanging open.

`"a"` means **append** — adds to the end without wiping. Looping directly over the file object gives you one line at a time (memory-friendly for big files). `line.strip()` trims the newline each line carries.

examples.title: Write, then read back:
examples.code:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("first line\n")
    f.write("second line\n")

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

examples.title: Append and read line by line:
examples.code:
with open("notes.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("third line\n")

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(">", line.strip())
examples.output:
> first line
> second line
> third line

exercises.task: Write a tiny log: every time the script runs, append the current date and time on its own line to log.txt.
exercises.hint: from datetime import datetime gives you datetime.now(). Open log.txt in append mode and write str(datetime.now()) plus a newline.

title: Errors, exceptions & debugging
subtitle: Read the letter, fix the bug
idea: An error message is a letter telling you exactly where it hurts. Read it bottom-up — last line first — and bugs stop being scary and start being instructions.

prose.text: Every programmer spends half their time reading errors. The pros aren't the ones who avoid them — they're the ones who **read the letter**. Python's traceback is genuinely helpful once you know where to look.

Read **bottom-up**: the last line names the error — `NameError: name 'totla' is not defined`. That's the diagnosis: you typed a name Python never saw. The line above it points at the exact line and even the column. The fix is spelling. Most tracebacks work exactly like this: last line = what, lines above = where.

`try` says "attempt this". `except ValueError` says "if *this specific thing* goes wrong, do that instead". Catch **specific** errors — a bare `except:` hides bugs you need to see. The pattern: try the risky thing, handle the failure you can predict, let everything else crash loudly so you learn about it.
The debugging checklist — tape this to the wall
**1. Read the LAST line first.** The error type and message are the diagnosis — everything above is just the address.
**2. Reproduce small.** The smallest input that still crashes is worth ten guesses.
**3. Print before the crash.** `print()` the value on the line *above* the failing one — most bugs are a value you didn't expect.
**4. Check the types.** `type(x)` settles half of all arguments about what's actually in a variable.
**5. Bisect.** Comment out half the code. Bug gone? It's in that half. Repeat until cornered.
**6. Walk away.** Ten minutes off beats an hour of staring — your brain keeps working without you.

examples.title: A crash, and how to read it:
examples.code:
total = 10 + 5
print(totla)
examples.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/tmp/course-verify-zyyeyt1k/main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(totla)
          ^^^^^
NameError: name 'totla' is not defined. Did you mean: 'total'?

title: Modules, packages & pip
subtitle: Import solved problems
idea: A .py file is a module the moment another file imports it. The standard library is thousands of solved problems — import before you build.

prose.text: You've been importing since lesson one without noticing (`type` and `print` are builtins, but `datetime` isn't). A **module** is just a `.py` file someone — including you — wrote. `import` loads it and hands you its contents.

`import random` brings the whole module; `from datetime import date` takes just one piece. The stdlib covers files, dates, math, randomness, the web, data formats — **check the stdlib before writing anything that feels generic**. It's already tested by millions.

`greet.py` became a module the instant `import greet` ran. Your projects grow exactly like this: one file gets crowded, you move a chunk into a new file, you import it. (That's also how your DDD tree is organized — `engines/`, `services/`, each file a module.)

examples.title: The standard library does the boring parts:
examples.code:
import random
from datetime import date

print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]))
print("year:", date.today().year)

examples.title: Your own module — two files, same folder:
examples.code:

exercises.task: Split any program you've written into two files: the logic in helpers.py, the running part in main.py.
exercises.hint: Move the defs into helpers.py, then in main.py: import helpers. Guard the running part with: if __name__ == "__main__": — that line means "only run this when the file is executed directly, not when it's imported".

title: Comprehensions & iteration
subtitle: Say more with less
idea: A comprehension builds a whole list or dict in one readable line. enumerate and zip let you loop with an index or in pairs — no hand-counting.

prose.text: You'll write a lot of loops that build lists. Python compresses that pattern into one line — a **comprehension**. It reads almost like English once you've seen three of them.

Read `[n * 2 for n in nums]` as "double each n, for each n in nums". The optional `if` filters. If a comprehension stops fitting on one line or needs two loops, **write the loop out** — readability beats cleverness, always.

`enumerate` hands you position + item together — no `i = 0` / `i += 1` bookkeeping. `zip` pairs two lists item-by-item. And dicts get comprehensions too: `{k: f"${v}" for k, v in prices.items()}` rebuilds the whole price list labeled.

examples.title: Loops, compressed:
examples.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
doubled = [n * 2 for n in nums]
evens = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
print(doubled)
print(evens)

title: Classes
subtitle: Only as much OOP as real code needs
idea: A class bundles data with the functions that operate on it. You need exactly this much: __init__ stores the data, methods use it, self means "this particular one".

prose.text: So far data (dicts) and behavior (functions) live apart. A **class** glues them: the invoice *knows* how to report its own status. You'll meet classes in every real codebase — including yours — so here's the working minimum.

`__init__` runs once when the object is born — it stores the data on `self`. Every method takes `self` first: it's how the method reaches *this particular* invoice's data. `inv = Invoice(...)` creates one; the class is the blueprint, `inv` is the building.
You've already read a real class: DDD's Service in services/service.py — __init__, methods, self, the same shape. Lesson 14 puts you inside it.

examples.title: Data that knows what to do:
examples.code:
class Invoice:
    def __init__(self, invoice_id, client, amount):
        self.invoice_id = invoice_id
        self.client = client
        self.amount = amount
        self.paid = False

    def mark_paid(self):
        self.paid = True

    def status(self):
        state = "PAID" if self.paid else "DUE"
        return f"{self.invoice_id} ({self.client}): ${self.amount} - {state}"

inv = Invoice("INV-1042", "Ava", 400)
print(inv.status())
inv.mark_paid()
print(inv.status())

exercises.task: Add a chase_message() method to Invoice that returns: "Hi {client}, invoice {id} for ${amount} is due."
exercises.hint: Methods take self first and read self.client, self.invoice_id, self.amount. It's one return line with an f-string.

title: Working with data
subtitle: CSV and JSON
idea: CSV is a spreadsheet as text. JSON is a dict as text. Nearly all real-world data arrives as one of these two — read them with the stdlib, never by hand.

prose.text: Invoices arrive as CSV. APIs answer in JSON. Configs live in JSON. Two formats, two stdlib modules, and you never parse either by splitting strings yourself — the edge cases will eat you.

`csv.DictReader` turns each row into a dictionary keyed by the header row — `row["client"]` instead of `row[1]`. Column order stops mattering. (The `newline=""` is a csv-module quirk — just include it.)

`json.dump` writes a Python dict/list straight to a file; `json.load` reads it back. JSON *is* dicts-and-lists as text — the mapping is one-to-one. `indent=2` makes it human-readable. This exact pattern (read CSV → filter → write JSON report) is real data work.

examples.title: Read a CSV by column name:
examples.code:
import csv

with open("invoices.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["client"], row["amount"], row["paid"])
examples.output:
Ava 400 no
Ben 150 yes
Cy 275 no

examples.title: Filter it, save the answer as JSON:
examples.code:
import csv, json

with open("invoices.csv", newline="") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

outstanding = [r for r in rows if r["paid"].strip().lower() != "yes"]
with open("report.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(outstanding, f, indent=2)

print(f"{len(outstanding)} outstanding:")
print(open("report.json").read())

exercises.task: Write only the rows with amount over 100 to expensive.csv, with the same header.
exercises.hint: csv.DictWriter needs fieldnames — grab them from the reader: reader.fieldnames. Remember writer.writeheader() before the rows, and compare with float(row["amount"]).

title: Automation
subtitle: Scripts, CLI args, schedules
idea: A script that takes arguments and runs on a schedule works while you sleep. That's a daemon's little cousin — and the shape of every DDD service.

prose.text: Scripts you've written so far have their settings baked in. Real automation takes **arguments** (`--days 7`) so one script serves many jobs, and runs on a **schedule** so nobody has to remember it.

`argparse` builds the `--help` text, checks types (`type=int` rejects `--days soon`), and fills defaults — for free. Run with `python3 chase.py --days 7`; run with no flags and `days` is 30. Every DDD service CLI (`--data-dir`, `--run-once`) is built exactly this way.
That's the whole automation stack: a script with arguments, a cron line, a log file. Your DDD services run this exact lifecycle — `run_once()` doing one unit of work, the schedule deciding *when*.

examples.title: A script that takes orders:
examples.code:
import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Chase overdue invoices.")
parser.add_argument("--days", type=int, default=30,
                    help="days overdue to chase")
args = parser.parse_args()

print(f"Chasing invoices {args.days}+ days overdue...")

examples.title: Put it on a schedule (Termux):
examples.code:
# In Termux:
#   pkg install cronie termux-services
#   sv-enable crond
#   crontab -e
#
# Add this line — every day at 9:00 AM:
#   0 9 * * * python3 ~/code/chase.py --days 7
#
# The five fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week.
# Logs go nowhere by default — append >> ~/code/chase.log 2>&1 to keep them.

exercises.hint: parser.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true") — no value needed, its presence sets args.dry_run to True. Then: if args.dry_run: print(...) else: do the thing.

title: Capstone
subtitle: Own your codebase
idea: The course ends where your real work lives: inside the DDD product tree at ~/workspace/ddd. Read it, change it, extend it, ship it.

prose.text: Everything so far was rehearsal. Your DDD tree — ten products, real CLIs, 126 tests — is written in exactly the Python you just learned. These five exercises move you from student to owner. Run them from `~/workspace/ddd`.
Exercise 1 — Read: find the templates

Open `services/invoicechaser.py`. Near the top you'll find `_TEMPLATES` — a dict keyed by `3, 7, 14, 30`, each value a `(subject, message)` tuple with `{client}`, `{invoice_id}`, `{amount}`, `{due}`, `{overdue}` placeholders. Below it, `run_once()` loops the CSV rows, skips paid invoices, picks the right step per row, and returns a **dict summary** of the run. Question to answer for yourself: what two things does the returned dict always contain? (Read the last three lines of `run_once`.)
Exercise 2 — Change: make the words yours
Edit the day-3 template's message text in `_TEMPLATES` — keep the `{placeholders}`, change the voice. Then run the demo and watch your words come out:
You just did the core loop of professional development: **change → run → observe**. Nothing about this required permission.
Exercise 3 — Add: your first service
Every DDD service implements the `Service` interface from `services/service.py` (Lesson 11's class pattern, for real). Create `services/shoutout.py`:
Then prove it works, from `~/workspace/ddd`:
Exercise 4 — Wire: add a --dry-run flag

Open the `main()` function at the bottom of `services/invoicechaser.py` — it's the argparse pattern from Lesson 13. Add `--dry-run` (`action="store_true"`), and when it's set, print the messages that *would* send instead of delivering them. Test both modes against `/tmp/ddd-cap/chaser`.
Exercise 5 — Ship: tests green, then commit

Done. You read production code, modified a live template, added a service implementing a real interface, extended a CLI, and shipped behind a green suite. That's not coursework anymore — that's the job.
